screeningScope: Full-text source, eligibility, study-design, taxonomy, and synthesis-readiness review of queue positions 1-12 after Batch 08 publication.

decisionDefinitions.INCLUDE: Eligible for evidence extraction and synthesis after full-text review.
decisionDefinitions.DEGRADED: A required source or verification element was unavailable.

records.sourceFile: Association of social media use on sleep quality and performance among collegiate athletes.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This cross-sectional study assessed 87 NCAA Division III track-and-field and swimming athletes at two colleges. Seven-day iPhone screen-time data, PROMIS sleep-disturbance scores, and public competition results showed worse sleep among athletes reporting more than five hours of daily social-media use than among those at two hours or less. Facebook time had a small adjusted association with failure to improve a season or personal best, while total social-media time did not independently predict that performance outcome.
records.limitations: The design cannot establish that social-media use caused sleep or performance differences. The small two-college sample was limited to track-and-field and swimming, relied on iPhone tracking and selected platforms, used a coarse competition-performance classification, and remains vulnerable to residual confounding and multiple-comparison findings.
records.synthesisCaution: Use the findings to prompt individualized conversations about digital routines and sleep, not to impose a universal screen-time cutoff or claim that reducing one platform will improve performance.

records.sourceFile: Does it matter - Isometric or isokinetic assessment of quadriceps strength symmetry 9 months after ACLR in collegiate athletes.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Thirty-five NCAA Division I athletes completed isometric and isokinetic quadriceps testing about nine months after ACL reconstruction, along with countermovement-jump, treadmill-running, and IKDC assessments. Mean limb-symmetry difference between modes was only 1.0%, but the individual limits of agreement were wide at -25.1% to 23.0%. Both modes related to functional knee kinetics, with generally stronger associations for isometric symmetry.
records.limitations: The preliminary sample was small, narrow, and mostly bone-patellar tendon-bone autografts from one Division I rehabilitation setting. All strength testing used an isokinetic dynamometer, possible fatigue from the testing battery was not eliminated, and the analysis could not adjust fully for sex, sport, graft, or concomitant procedures.
records.synthesisCaution: Either contraction mode can support assessment, but the wide individual limits mean values should not be treated as interchangeable within an athlete. Keep the testing mode consistent and combine strength symmetry with kinetics, symptoms, function, and sport exposure.

records.sourceFile: Impact of Sled Loads on Performance and Kinematics of Elite Sprinters and Rugby Players.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Eight elite male sprinters and ten rugby-union players completed 20-m sprints while towing 0%, 20%, and 60% of body mass. Sprint splits and lower-limb kinematics showed that the same relative sled loads produced different velocity decrements and technique changes between groups; differences also depended on whether the load was 20% or 60% of body mass.
records.limitations: This was an acute, cross-sectional comparison of only 18 elite male athletes over 20 m. The groups performed on their sport-specific surfaces and footwear, and the study did not test longitudinal adaptation, longer sprint phases, injury, or whether the observed acute mechanics predict training response.
records.synthesisCaution: Do not transfer a body-mass percentage unchanged across sports or athletes. Use observed velocity loss and technical response to individualize the overload, then verify adaptation longitudinally.

records.sourceFile: Importance of Various Training-Load Measures in Injury Incidence of Professional Rugby League Athletes.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Daily internal and external training-load and injury-status data were analyzed for 25 professional rugby-league players across three seasons using generalized estimating equations and random forests. The most important load features differed by positional group and by athlete, with combinations of total distance, high-metabolic-power distance, session-RPE load, and rolling windows contributing differently.
records.limitations: The observational data came from one professional club with 25 players, so feature importance may reflect that team's exposures, definitions, and workflows. Repeated load observations and flexible individual models can overfit, and associations with injury status do not establish causal thresholds or prove prospective decision benefit in another squad.
records.synthesisCaution: Treat the reported variables as evidence for individualized, position-aware monitoring rather than universal injury cut points. Any model or alert rule requires local prospective validation and clinical interpretation.

records.sourceFile: Individual in-situ GPS derived accleration speed profiling - Toward automatization and refinement in male professional rugby union players.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: The study automated in-situ acceleration-speed profiling for 49 male professional rugby-union players using 61.5 million GPS positions from 51 training sessions and 11 matches. Individual relationships were linear (all R-squared greater than 0.81), two-week reliability ranged from ICC 0.72 to 0.92 with SEM of 4.2% to 8.6%, and profile components varied by position and session type.
records.limitations: Profile quality depends on the GPS data and on acceleration derived from changes in GPS speed rather than the embedded accelerometer. The theoretical intercepts are modeled rather than directly achieved maxima, reliability was studied in one male professional setting, and the paper did not validate profile-guided decisions against injury, return-to-sport, or performance outcomes.
records.synthesisCaution: Use the method as an ecological profiling and monitoring layer with its error estimates visible. Do not equate a theoretical intercept with a directly tested maximum or use it alone for injury prediction or return-to-sport clearance.

records.sourceFile: Inertial flywheel knee and hip dominant hamstring strength exercises in professional soccer players - Muscle use and velocity based eccentric overload.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Eighteen elite male professional soccer players completed an acute four-set, eight-repetition session of either flywheel leg curl or conic-pulley hip extension. Encoder measures and pre/post functional MRI showed exercise-specific mechanical and regional hamstring responses: leg curl emphasized overall semitendinosus and short-head biceps femoris use, while hip extension emphasized proximal and medial long-head biceps femoris; eccentric overload was not uniform across metrics.
records.limitations: The small acute study used MRI T2 change as a metabolic proxy for muscle use, included athletes inexperienced with inertial devices, and did not measure longitudinal strength, hypertrophy, sprinting, injury, or reinjury. Tendon and elastic contributions can also alter the relationship between T2 response and muscle work.
records.synthesisCaution: Use the findings to select exercises for different regional emphases and to plan familiarization, not as proof that one exercise prevents hamstring injury or repairs a specific injured region.

records.sourceFile: Do sports compression garments alter measures of peripheral blood flow - A systematic review with meta-analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: A random-effects meta-analysis of 22 studies found a small overall increase in peripheral blood-flow measures with sports compression garments (SMD 0.32, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.51), driven particularly by venous flow. Effects varied by timing: flow improved during a physiological challenge, venous flow improved at rest and in recovery, and no immediate post-challenge overall effect was detected.
records.limitations: The included studies used 23 blood-flow measures and varied garments, pressures, timepoints, challenges, and methods. Blinding and garment-pressure verification were commonly limited, overall methodological quality was moderate, and the review team received a research grant from a compression-garment manufacturer, though the authors reported no sponsor role in analysis or publication.
records.synthesisCaution: A small change in a blood-flow surrogate is not proof of better recovery or performance. If garments are used, verify fit and pressure, athlete tolerance, timing, and the outcome that actually matters.

records.sourceFile: Does resisted sprint training improve the sprint performance of field-based invasion team sport players - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Across 21 studies, resisted sprint training produced similar between-group sprint improvements to unresisted sprinting in field-based invasion-sport players. Within resisted-training groups, early acceleration improved more (SMD -0.80) than late acceleration (SMD -0.28), with no detected maximum-velocity improvement; light and very heavy loads both improved early acceleration.
records.limitations: The strongest conclusion is equivalence to unresisted sprinting, while several favorable estimates came from within-group change. Studies varied in loading method, velocity decrement, sport, concurrent team training, intervention design, and risk of bias, making a single optimal load unsupported.
records.synthesisCaution: Use resisted sprinting as one effective acceleration option, not as a proven replacement for free sprinting or maximum-velocity exposure. Prescribe by the intended velocity decrement and athlete response rather than labels such as light or very heavy alone.

records.sourceFile: Efects of Warm‑Up, Post‑Warm‑Up, and Re‑Warm‑Up Strategies on Explosive Eforts in Team Sports- A Systematic Review.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This systematic review included 30 team-sport studies of warm-up, the transition before play, and re-warm-up. Shorter progressive warm-ups with dynamic and explosive tasks generally supported sprint, jump, and agility performance; heated garments helped preserve readiness during inactive transitions, and brief explosive re-warm-ups were most useful when delays exceeded about 15 minutes or at halftime.
records.limitations: Protocols, intensities, durations, recovery periods, sports, control conditions, and outcomes varied widely. Several recommendations depended on single studies, and the authors could not meta-analyze or establish one optimal protocol across sports and populations.
records.synthesisCaution: Treat the proposed 10-15 minute structure, heat-retention, and re-warm-up options as starting templates. Adjust them to the sport's rules, environment, athlete needs, and actual transition duration.

records.sourceFile: Effect of movement velocity during      resistance training on dynamic muscular strength - A systematic review    and   meta-analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Fifteen comparative studies involving 509 participants found similar dynamic-strength gains from fast and moderate-slow resistance-training velocities when intensities were pooled. At moderate loads of 60-79% 1RM, faster training showed only a small favorable trend (effect size 0.31, p=0.06), not a conventionally significant advantage.
records.limitations: Studies varied in load, intended and actual movement velocity, participant age and training status, exercise selection, and intervention duration; more than half lasted only six to eight weeks. The broad sample makes athlete-specific conclusions uncertain, and the moderate-load subgroup result was a nonsignificant trend.
records.synthesisCaution: Do not present fast repetitions as universally superior for strength. Match intent and velocity to load, exercise, safety, and adaptation goals while preserving progressive overload and execution quality.

records.sourceFile: Effects of acute sleep deprivation on sporting performance in athletes - A comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: A meta-analysis of 27 studies and 75 performance indicators found an overall adverse effect of acute sleep deprivation (effect size -0.56). Reported effects were largest for high-intensity intermittent exercise and skill control, followed by speed, aerobic endurance, and explosive power; late-night or early-morning sleep loss and afternoon testing produced larger estimates in some subgroup analyses.
records.limitations: The synthesis was constrained by the quantity and quality of the underlying studies, heterogeneous deprivation protocols and performance indicators, and sparse subgroups, including some with only two indicators. The outcome classification and repeated indicators may overstate precision, and time-of-day subgroup findings should not be treated as universal causal rules.
records.synthesisCaution: Prioritize preventing acute sleep loss rather than trying to optimize around it. When unavoidable, reduce decision-critical or high-intensity demands where possible and use individual symptoms and performance checks; do not turn subgroup estimates into travel or competition guarantees.

records.sourceFile: Effects of bilateral and unilateral resistance training on horizontally orientated movement performance - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Eleven studies showed that both bilateral and unilateral resistance training improved horizontally oriented movement performance (bilateral SMD 0.60; unilateral SMD 0.57). There was no meaningful difference between modes (SMD 0.17, 95% CI -0.15 to 0.50), and combined resistance-plus-plyometric approaches tended to produce larger effects than strength work alone.
records.limitations: Between-study heterogeneity was moderate, included outcomes and programs varied, and subgroup analyses dichotomized continuous variables and tested moderators independently. Those choices reduce power and cannot resolve interactions among load, exercise type, experience, and program design.
records.synthesisCaution: Choose bilateral and unilateral work according to loading capacity, stability, symptoms, movement goals, and athlete preference. The review supports using both; it does not establish one universally superior mode.
